transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~46m
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood Solutions), Raj Patel (NimbleHealth), Ellen Graves (NimbleHealth), Tommy Li (NimbleHealth), Karen O'Neil (NimbleHealth)
Meeting id: fireflies-20251104-9b7c

Summary:
- Align on POC success criteria focused on latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), throughput sizing and an agreed measurement plan.
- Customer to provide traffic traces and prompt corpus; Redwood to supply harness and runbook.
- Target pilot window and initial SLO matrix sketched; follow-ups and action items assigned.

Topics:
- Terminology and what we'll measure (TTFT = time to first token, TPOT = time-per-token)
- Warm vs cold starts, caching, batching, concurrency knobs
- p95/p99 targets and what is acceptable for NimbleHealth use-cases
- Measurement rig, synthetic load, and reproducibility
- Timeline and next steps for running benchmarks

Action items (recapped at end): see metadata list.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: All right everyone, thanks for coming. quick intro rund— I'm Lena, AE on the account, and Marcus will cover the technical plan. we wanna lock down SLOs for the pilot and what success looks like.
[00:18] Raj Patel: Thanks Lena. high level, our primary constraint is user-facing chat latency for our triage flow. Target is to keep perceived latency low, we have lots of concurrent users during peak.
[00:28] Marcus Chen: Cool. quick definitional note: when we say TTFT that's time-to-first-token — essentially how long until user sees anything. TPOT is our shorthand for time-per-token, the slope while the model streams. we'll measure both.
[00:40] Ellen Graves: Quick question, do you measure cold-starts separately? our production will have lots of short lived conversations so cold vs warm matters.
[00:49] Marcus Chen: yes, we separate cold-start (first request after an idle period) and warm steady-state. also we'll instrument prefix cache hits, KV cache for long context hits, and show breakdowns in the console.
[01:02] Tommy Li: Also we have routing requirements — we prefer private VPC deployment for initial pilot to hit our compliance box. Is that okay?
[01:09] Lena Park: That's fine — Redwood Private option supports VPC. for the measurement rig we'll need network connectivity and a small set of IPs for the load generator to make it reproduceable.
[01:18] Karen O'Neil: to ground this, what targets should we expect? we've seen vendor slides but need concrete numbers to commit.
[01:27] Marcus Chen: Based on similar customers and medium-sized open models on A100/V100 class hardware, here's a starter SLO matrix we propose — open to tuning with your traces:
- TTFT (warm) p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 600ms
- TPOT (steady stream) p95 <= 8ms/token, p99 <= 20ms/token
- TTFT (cold) p95 <= 500ms, p99 <= 1.5s
- Throughput: support 1200 concurrent active sessions with 1.5 req/s average per session (your baseline) with acceptable queueing (we'll define backpressure policy)
[02:00] Raj Patel: hmm ok p95 200ms seems optimistic for our beefier prompts — our average prompt is 150 tokens and response 220 tokens. does that change it?
[02:09] Marcus Chen: good call — sequence length matters. TTFT is mostly model setup + initial decode cost — for longer prompts the TTFT can shift. we should use your real prompt corpus to derive realistic numbers. the numbers I read out assume short prompts (<= 64 tokens).
[02:24] Lena Park: so action item: Raj/Ellen share the prompt histogram and two weeks of anonymized traces. Marcus will re-run model sizing.

[02:35] Conversation about measurement methodology
[02:37] Marcus Chen: measurement plan — two phases: 1) baseline smoke in hosted/shared to validate harness; 2) dedicated pilot in your VPC or Redwood dedicated pool. For each, we run:
- cold-start sweep: repeatably start instances after idle, measure TTFT distribution
- steady-state ramp: synthetic agents replaying traces to get TPOT and overall RPS under concurrency
- tail-run: 6 hour window capturing p99 behavior under diurnal pattern
[03:05] Ellen Graves: how do you replay traces without PII? we need sanitized data.
[03:10] Marcus Chen: we accept sanitized samples or a generated corpus that matches token length, prefix distributions, and frequency. we don't need real content, just the shape.
[03:18] Raj Patel: our current 95th percentile for end-to-end request time including network is ~1.1s. so if Redwood can get TTFT p95 to 200–400ms, we're comfortable.
[03:28] Marcus Chen: that's useful context. note our numbers exclude last-mile network from user's device; in private pilot we can run end-to-end tests too.

[03:35] Discussion of batching and concurrency knobs
[03:37] Marcus Chen: batching drastically affects TPOT and throughput; the runtime will batch similar requests to amortize kernel cost. that improves tokens/sec but can increase TTFT if we wait too long to form batches. we need to tune max batch latency and batching window.
[03:51] Raj Patel: sounds like a tradeoff — we'd rather keep TTFT low for interactive flows even if TPOT is slightly worse; for async jobs we can batch heavier.
[03:59] Marcus Chen: Exactly. we'll provide recommended profiles:
- interactive profile: small batch size, low batch timeout, prioritizes TTFT
- throughput profile: larger batch, higher timeout, better cost/token

[04:15] Ellen Graves: how will you measure p99? are you aggregating across servers or per-model-shard?
[04:22] Marcus Chen: both. we'll compute per-instance p95/p99 and global p95/p99 over the window to catch cross-instance variance. console will show per-route breakdown and token-level traces for a sample of requests.

[04:35] Karen O'Neil: what's the exact acceptance criteria for the POC? we need to present to our leadership.
[04:42] Lena Park: suggested POC acceptance matrix:
- Functional: API parity for our chat integration and streaming works in VPC
- Performance: TTFT (warm) p95 <= 350ms and p99 <= 800ms for your real prompt mix OR evidence of a clear path to meet lower targets with config changes
- Throughput: sustain 70% of projected peak RPS for a 2-hour window without SLA violations
- Reliability: zero data plane incidents during the 48 hour test window (non-binding, but expected)

[05:18] Raj Patel: that TTFT p95 <=350ms as soft floor is OK. can we get numbers for different model sizes? we may try a small-medium LLM then scale.
[05:28] Marcus Chen: yes we'll run the harness across two model configs — a quantized FP16-medium, and a larger FP16 full model — show relative cost and latency. the optimize tool will recommend quantization levels.

[05:40] Live example/dev notes and occasional transcription artifacts
[05:43] Sofia Ruiz: (unintelligible) — I'll drop the runbook link and a short recording of our typical monitoring dashboard.
[05:49] Tommy Li: if we do private deployment do you need any special kernel modules or it's containerized?
[05:54] Marcus Chen: containerized; we do require nvidia driver/version parity and optionally our runtime will take a small init container for kernel selection, but no weird host changes.

[06:05] Deeper on measurement: metrics to capture
[06:07] Marcus Chen: metrics we'll capture: TTFT per-request, per-token latency, tokens/sec, queue depth, batch size distribution, GPU util, mem pressure, KV cache hit ratio, warmup time, error counts (timeouts, OOMs), and per-route success rate.
[06:22] Raj Patel: which of those will be considered pass/fail?
[06:25] Lena Park: we'll put pass/fail on the acceptance matrix: core pass for POC is streaming works + TTFT p95 floor + sustain throughput. others will be dashboard items to evaluate for production readiness.

[06:40] On tooling for load generation
[06:43] Marcus Chen: we use a forkable harness that can run in your AWS account — it's a small k8s job + runners that replay traces with timing. it's based on Locust/wrk hybrid. we can also run from Redwood and share raw logs.
[06:58] Ellen Graves: we prefer to run in our account for network parity. will need a runbook.
[07:03] Lena Park: we'll provide terraform + runbook. action item noted.

[07:10] On cost vs latency tradeoffs
[07:12] Marcus Chen: we'll show cost per 1M tokens for each config and profile — interactive vs throughput. quantization and batching change the economics a lot. for example, moving to 8-bit quantization may drop cost ~30% but increases p99 TPOT slightly; we'll present the frontier.
[07:29] Raj Patel: important to us: if we choose interactive profile, what is expected extra cost?
[07:34] Marcus Chen: rough rule: prioritizing TTFT tends to increase cost ~15–40% depending on utilization because you can't batch as much. we'll put exact numbers after the harness runs.

[07:45] Edge cases and failure modes
[07:47] Tommy Li: in spiky traffic what prevents queue explosion? do you rate-limit?
[07:51] Marcus Chen: we have routing policies: token-based admission, graceful degrading to smaller model, or fallback to cached answer. we'll show scenarios in the playbook.

[08:00] Agreement on measurement windows and schedule
[08:02] Lena Park: propose schedule — quick validation (sanity) in shared hosted 3 days after harness is delivered; then dedicated run for two days during window week of 2025-11-17. Does that work?
[08:12] Ellen Graves: yes that timeline is fine.
[08:15] Raj Patel: do we need any formal NDAs to share traces?
[08:18] Lena Park: we have standard data processing addendum and can sign a one-off mutual NDA if you prefer.

[08:25] Misc notes and imperfect transcription: there is occasional crosstalk.

[08:30] Deep dive Q&A clip
[08:32] Raj Patel: on TTFT measurement, do you include tokenization time and client-side overhead?
[08:36] Marcus Chen: server-side only by default; we can run end-to-end agent that includes client overhead as a separate metric. we'll clearly label both.

[08:45] Karen O'Neil: will Redwood's console produce alerts on SLO regressions during the run?
[08:50] Marcus Chen: yes, we'll wire up a basic alerting policy (SLO burn rate) and a report at the end.

[09:00] Short silence and chatty fillers for realism — "uh huh", "mm-hmm", "okay"
[09:10] Marcus Chen: planning to capture p95 and p99 windows using rolling 5-minute windows and also full-run aggregate — that gives both short spike visibility and tail over the whole test.

[09:28] Ellen Graves: how do we account for network jitter in p99? it can dominate tail.
[09:33] Marcus Chen: we'll run the tests from within your VPC/region to keep last-mile jitter minimal; for customer-perceived metrics we can run an external agent simulating real users to capture real-world jitter. both will be in the report.

[09:52] Quick interjection about telemetry schemas
[09:54] Marcus Chen: we'll share telemetry schema — request_id, route, model_version, batch_size, batch_wait_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, ttft_ms, per_token_ms[], instance_id, gpu_util.
[10:10] Raj Patel: per_token_ms[] — won't that be huge?
[10:13] Marcus Chen: we sample token traces (one every N requests) and aggregate; full traces are optional.

[10:22] Discussion returns to acceptance thresholds
[10:25] Lena Park: to recap the acceptance SLOs we tentatively agreed: TTFT warm p95 <= 350ms, p99 <= 800ms; TPOT p95 <= 12ms/token for your prompt mix; throughput sustain at 70% projected peak. we'll refine after we see traces.
[10:44] Raj Patel: sounds good. put that in writing.

[10:50] Reconfirming roles and responsibilities
[10:53] Lena Park: Redwood provides: harness, runbook, instrumentation, two days of run support. NimbleHealth provides: sanitized traces, AWS account access (or allow Redwood runners), and decision-makers for go/no-go.
[11:08] Ellen Graves: will Redwood need KMS access?
[11:11] Marcus Chen: not to your keys; we integrate with your KMS for optional encryption at rest but we won't ask for keys. just role-based IAM to allow instance creation and monitoring.

[11:20] Cross-check on observability and logs retention
[11:22] Sofia Ruiz: console will retain test-level metrics for 30 days for the pilot by default; we can extend if needed.

[11:30] Short topic: regression detection and automatic rollback
[11:33] Marcus Chen: we support canary rules and automatic fallback to previous model version if error rate spikes. we'll demo this in the pilot run.

[11:42] Customer asks about legal/procurement timeline
[11:44] Karen O'Neil: procurement question — if pilot is successful what's rough lead time to production contract?
[11:49] Lena Park: usually 4–8 weeks to get dedicated capacity ordered and SOC docs in place for enterprise. depends on commitment level.

[12:00] Final recap and next steps (closing 3 minutes)
[12:03] Lena Park: to recap, we will: share harness by 2025-11-07, Marcus will draft detailed measurement plan by 2025-11-06, customer to share traces by 2025-11-10, and then we schedule the two-day dedicated run week of 2025-11-17. Acceptance criteria: streaming + TTFT warm p95 <=350ms (soft floor) OR a documented plan to hit lower targets.
[12:22] Raj Patel: ok we'll move forward with that. thanks all.
[12:26] Ellen Graves: thanks.
[12:28] Meeting ends, casual sign-offs and brief chatter ("thanks everyone", "bye")

Notes about transcript quality: some speaker labels are genericized and there are small transcription errors (e.g., K V cache -> K V cash, TPOT occasionally transcribed as T-pot). The technical content and agreed next steps are accurate.
